name: THE PEA-BRIE'S BIG ADVENTURE BURGER (Pea Protein Burger w/Brie)

recipe.history:
The garden pea — Pisum sativum — has been cultivated for at least ten thousand years, with archaeological evidence of its cultivation found at sites in the Near East and along the ancient Silk Road trading routes. It arrived in Europe through Greece and Rome, where dried peas were a staple of the legionary diet, and by the Middle Ages it had become one of the most important crops in Northern European agriculture. Modern pea protein isolate emerged from a very different tradition: the industrial processing of yellow split peas for their protein content, a technology developed in earnest in the early 2000s when food scientists began searching for plant-based protein sources that could replicate the texture and binding properties of meat. Canada became the world's largest producer of field peas partly for this reason, and today pea protein is the foundation of several major plant-based burger brands. It is high in lysine, relatively neutral in flavor compared to soy, and binds moisture in ways that make it uniquely suited to forming a patty with a crust that browns under heat.

Brie cheese, from the Île-de-France region east of Paris, is the product of a completely different civilization's genius: the art of bloomy-rind soft-ripened cheese, in which Penicillium camemberti mold is cultivated on the surface of fresh cow's milk cheese to create a white, powdery rind that slowly enzymes the paste from the outside in, transforming it over weeks into the runny, buttery, mushroomy interior that defines the great Bries of La Ferté and Meaux. Brie de Meaux has been produced since at least the eighth century CE and was famously called the "King of Cheeses" at the Congress of Vienna in 1815, when diplomats from across Europe ranked it above all other varieties. In the American plant-based burger space, pairing Brie with a pea protein patty makes perfect intellectual sense: both are innovations in transforming humble ingredients — peas, fresh milk — into something far more complex than their origins suggest.

I am not, by nature, a plant-based burger convert. I have eaten too many patties that tasted of protein powder and desperation to approach the category with anything but wariness. But the summer I spent experimenting with pea protein and beet juice and methylcellulose in my own kitchen, I found a combination that genuinely surprised me — a patty that browned properly, held together without falling apart, and had a mild green earthiness that was its own flavor rather than an apology for the absence of beef. The Brie was a late addition, suggested by a friend who pointed out that the fat content of a ripe Brie is high enough to compensate for what plant-based patties lack — that unctuousness, that sense of richness slowly releasing as you bite down. She was right. The combination felt less like health food and more like something you would eat by choice.

Cooking any patty — pea protein or beef — to the right internal temperature is an act of respect for the ingredients. For this pea protein patty, the target is the same 130–135°F (54–57°C) that I hold as inviolable for beef: this temperature ensures that the methylcellulose and protein matrix have set properly so the patty holds its shape, the beet juice has caramelized at the exterior to produce a convincing mahogany crust, and the interior remains moist and yielding rather than dry and crumbly. The Brie placed on top needs this precise warmth to begin softening: at 54–57°C, the cheese starts weeping its internal paste at the cut edge, flowing slightly down the sides of the patty in a way that makes each bite a small event. Under- or over-shoot the temperature and the entire effect collapses — either the patty is structurally unstable or the cheese sits cold and unyielding atop something dry.
ingredients: 3 large eggs (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
For the pea shoot and mint salad:
Salt and white pepper to taste
300g ripe Brie, rind on, sliced into 6 portions
instructions: 1. Make the pea protein patties (prepare at least 1 hour ahead): Combine pea protein isolate, methylcellulose, smoked paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, black pepper, and kosher salt in a large bowl and whisk to blend. Add beet juice, melted coconut oil, and soy sauce, then stir. Add cold water gradually, mixing with a fork, until the mixture comes together in a firm, moldable dough that holds its shape when pressed. Add water sparingly — the mixture should be moist but not sticky. Divide into 6 equal portions of roughly 130g each, form into 10cm-wide, 1.5cm-thick patties with a slight indent in the center. Refrigerate on a parchment-lined tray for at least 1 hour to firm up.

2. Make the brioche buns: Combine bread flour, instant yeast, salt, and sugar in a stand mixer bowl with a dough hook. Add 2 eggs and warm milk, mix on low for 2 minutes. Knead on medium for 5 minutes. Add softened butter one tablespoon at a time, fully incorporating each addition. Knead on medium-high for 8 minutes until smooth and elastic.

3. Place dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and let rise 1 hour until doubled. Divide into 6 portions of about 100g, shape into tight balls, set on a parchment-lined baking sheet, and proof covered for 45 minutes.
4. Preheat oven to 190°C (375°F). Brush buns with egg wash (remaining egg plus 1 tablespoon water) and bake 16–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a wire rack.
5. Make the Dijon cream sauce: Stir together crème fraîche, whole-grain Dijon, lemon juice, and honey until smooth. Season with salt and white pepper. Refrigerate until needed.
6. Make the pea shoot salad: Just before assembly, combine pea shoots and torn mint in a bowl. Whisk olive oil and lemon juice together, season with salt and pepper, and toss with the greens.

7. Cook the pea protein patties: Heat a non-stick skillet or well-seasoned cast-iron pan over medium-high heat. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Cook the chilled patties undisturbed for 4 minutes on the first side until a dark, crispy crust forms. Flip carefully with a wide spatula. Immediately place a portion of Brie on each patty. Cover the pan with a lid and cook for 3–4 more minutes. Check internal temperature with an instant-read thermometer — target is 130–135°F (54–57°C) at the center. The Brie should be visibly softening and beginning to flow at the edges. Rest for 2 minutes.
8. Slice brioche buns and toast cut-side down in a lightly buttered skillet over medium heat for 60–90 seconds.

9. Assemble each burger: Spread Dijon cream sauce generously on both cut faces of the bun. Layer tomato slices and shallot rings on the bottom bun. Place the rested pea protein patty with its softened Brie on top. Crown with a generous handful of the pea shoot and mint salad. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt and the top bun. Serve immediately while the Brie is still warm and yielding.
